references.text: Moses wrote down all the Lord's words, which corresponds to the command to write down the words in Exodus 34:27.
The Book of the Covenant was read to the people, and the covenant was made between the Lord and Israel through blood, paralleling the covenant-making mentioned in Exodus 34:27.
The Lord commanded Moses to carve out new stone tablets, which is the context for writing down the words in verse 27.
Moses wrote the ten words on the tablets, which is the direct fulfillment of the command in verse 27.
The Lord proclaimed His covenant and the Ten Commandments that He wrote on two stone tablets, paralleling the covenant-making in Exodus 34:27.
Moses wrote down this law and gave it to the priests, reflecting the command to write down the words.
Joshua made a covenant with the people and wrote the words in the Book of God's Law, which is a parallel to Moses' recording of the covenant words.
Jeremiah received the command to write down all the words the Lord had spoken, a parallel to the command given to Moses.
The Letter to the Hebrews refers to the better covenant established on better promises, contrasting the old covenant (Exodus 34:27) with the new covenant.
Reference to the blood of the covenant and Moses' role in making the covenant, linking it to the covenant mentioned in Exodus 34:27.
Contextual and theological connection: The written law (tablets) is the concrete foundation for the covenant mentioned in both verses.
Theological contrast and fulfillment: The external written covenant (Exodus) meets the internal covenant of the heart (Hebrews).
Direct narrative connection: Both verses define the covenant as based on the same 'words' at Sinai.
Prophetic contrast: The external written covenant (Exodus) is set in perspective by the internal covenant of the heart (Jeremiah).
